title: Speech and breath argue about who is greatest (1.2)
hook: the senses quarrel over which of them matters most, and they settle it by leaving the body one at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday: the udgitha, om, the high song, and your line, the essence. Earth, water, plants, person, speech, verse, chant, om. Did you find the rasa of one ordinary thing? Day three hundred thirty-three.

Sooner or later, a team has this argument. The person who talks to the clients says the whole company runs on them. The person who builds the product says nothing exists without them. The planner says without a plan it's all chaos. Everyone is a little bit right, and nobody wants to hear it. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story about the same fight, only the team is inside your own body. Speech, the eye, the ear, the mind, and the breath, all arguing about which of them is the greatest. And the way they settle it is brilliant, and a little brutal.
screen: `EVERY TEAM HAS THIS ARGUMENT.` → `THE TEAM IS YOUR BODY.` → `WHO IS THE GREATEST?`

segments.voice: The senses go to Prajapati, the lord of creatures, and ask him to judge. He gives them a test: the greatest is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off. So they take turns walking out. Speech leaves for a whole year. When it comes back it asks, how did you manage without me? The others say: like someone who can't speak. We breathed, we saw, we heard, we thought. We got by. Then the eye leaves for a year, and they get by like someone who can't see. The ear leaves, and they live like someone who can't hear. The mind leaves, and they live, the text says, like small children whose minds haven't grown yet. Each time, the body carries on. Then breath gets ready to go. And the text gives the picture that makes this story stick: as a strong horse, pulling away, tears up the pegs it was tethered to, the breath begins to tear up all the others with it. Speech, eye, ear and mind come running. Stay, they say. You're the greatest of us. This full story sits in chapter five of the Chandogya. In chapter one, the passage the outline points to, a shorter story makes the same point: gods and demons fight, the demons spoil speech, eye, ear and mind with evil, but when they strike the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they shatter like a clod of earth thrown at a rock. In both places, breath is the one that holds the rest. And chapter five ends by saying people don't call the senses speech, eyes, ears and minds. They call them all pranas, breaths.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TEST: WHO CAN LEAVE?` · `SPEECH, EYE, EAR, MIND: THE BODY GETS BY.` · `THE HORSE TEARS UP ITS PEGS.` · `THE SENSES ARE CALLED BREATHS.` · then, large: `STAY. YOU'RE THE GREATEST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice gives the senses the day off and keeps the breath. Sit and settle. Let your eyes close: the eye has stepped out, and you're still here. Let the room's sounds go to the background: the ear has stepped out too. Stay silent: no speech. Let thoughts drift past without chasing them. And notice what's still going, without being asked. In, and out. The one the others ran back to. Just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Speech and breath argue about who is greatest. The senses leave the body one by one; when breath starts to leave, all the others are torn up with it.
Your line: breath wins. Today, if you find yourself in an argument about who matters most, at work or at home, take one slow breath before you speak. Day three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama, the regulation of breath, as part of daily worship and yoga; teachers sometimes tell this story of breath as the chief of the senses alongside it.

match.prompt: who left, and how the body got by — tap the pairs.

myth: in the story, the body dies when speech leaves
speech is gone a whole year, and the body gets by, like someone who can't speak.
the text compares breath to a horse tearing up its tethering pegs
as breath starts to go, it pulls the other senses up with it.
the text says the senses are all called pranas, breaths
breath holds the rest, so the Chandogya says people name them all after it.

fork.setup: you're Prajapati. the senses want you to say which of them is greatest. how do you judge?
options: let each one leave the body for a while, and see whose absence hurts most.
say they're all equal and send them home.
fork.reveal: the test is absence. speech, eye, ear and mind each leave for a year and the body manages. when breath starts to go, everything comes with it.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, life-breath. the Chandogya says the senses are all called prāṇas, after their chief.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about the body's parts, like a children's story.
what it means: a test of absence. every sense can leave and the body carries on, except breath, which holds all the others.
what a scholar hears: the full dispute is Chandogya 5.1 (and Brihadaranyaka 6.1); 1.2 tells the gods-and-demons version, where evil can't touch the chief breath.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 5.1.6–12 (the senses' dispute; the horse and the pegs)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.2 (gods and demons; the clod against the rock)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 1.2 summary corrected (the demons spoil the nose-breath too; it is the breath in the mouth, the chief breath, they cannot touch); 'the senses are often called pranas' now attributed to the text (5.1.15); 'every team' hook softened; howItsDone no longer claims the story is a root of pranayama.

The outline cites 1.2, but the dispute among the senses described by the title is told in full at Chandogya 5.1 (and Brihadaranyaka 6.1). The script tells 5.1 and names 1.2's gods-and-demons version; suggest the outline reference read '(1.2; 5.1)'.
Order of departures in 5.1 (speech, eye, ear, mind) and the 'like small children' detail for mind: confirm.
